According to Robb Report, this Eagle Drive mansion in Jupiter was built in 1998 for Celine Dion and her late husband, René Angélil. The publication identifies its style as Mediterranean. For us, that origin provides an intriguing introduction, rather than the sole reason to give the property attention.
Scale With a Counterpoint

Robb Report puts the house at approximately 14,750 square feet on roughly two-thirds of an acre. Those figures offer an interesting contrast: a substantial mansion without an acreage-led identity. Its appeal, on paper, rests more on the spaces within and their relationship to the water.
A Room That Embraces Drama

The private theater features red velvet seating, a coffered ceiling and a crystal chandelier, the publication reports. Our favorite detail is that unabashedly theatrical combination. Rather than treating entertainment as a purely technical amenity, the room’s reported decorative elements give it a distinct visual personality.
The Waterfront Chapter

Outside, Robb Report describes a pool and hot tub overlooking the water, a covered patio with an outdoor kitchen, and a private dock providing waterway access. The dock is the standout for us: it adds a practical boating dimension alongside the estate’s more exuberant indoor features.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A London Water Tower With a New Perspective
illustrationDraft.deck: Victorian brickwork, a glass-and-steel addition and a former water tank turned lookout give this London conversion its distinctive architectural rhythm.
paragraphs: Infrastructure, Reconsidered

According to Robb Report, this tower was built in the 1860s to supply the nearby Lambeth Workhouse and converted into a roughly 4,500-square-foot residence in 2011. Its appeal lies in that dramatic change of purpose: an imposing piece of civic infrastructure rethought at a domestic scale.
A Deliberate Contrast

Robb Report describes Venetian Gothic brickwork paired with an ultramodern glass-and-steel extension called the Cube. Its ground floor contains an open-plan kitchen and dining room alongside a reception room with full-height sliding glass doors. Architecturally, the contrast is more compelling than an attempt to make the addition disappear.
A Home That Climbs

The report identifies an original York stone staircase connecting the floors, plus a separate added elevator tower. Five bedrooms and four bathrooms occupy the tower. That vertical arrangement suggests a different domestic rhythm from a sprawling mansion, with movement between levels central to the design.
The Tank Becomes the Destination

At the top, Robb Report places the Prospect Room inside the original cast-iron water tank, with windows on all four sides and views including the London Eye. This is the conversion’s strongest idea: giving the tower’s defining industrial component a new role rather than treating it as a relic.
